title: How to Use Cloudflare Workers (2026 Beginner Guide)
summary: How to use Cloudflare Workers to write a JavaScript function and deploy it instantly. You'll get a public workers.dev URL in about ten minutes.
body_markdown:
## Custom domains, secrets, and storage for a Worker


Attach a custom domain from your own Cloudflare zone, store credentials with` wrangler secret put` , and choose KV, D1 or R2 by what you're saving. Each is a one-line fix when it goes wrong.


### Custom domain versus workers.dev


On a custom domain, the Worker is the origin for a hostname like` api.example.com` . Cloudflare creates the DNS record and certificate for you, provided the domain's DNS is already on Cloudflare.


If you use a route instead, the Worker sits in front of a hostname that already has an origin server, matching a pattern such as` example.com/api/*` . That means a route silently does nothing if the hostname isn't proxied.


Use a custom domain for a new service and a route when you're adding logic to an existing site.


Run` wrangler secret put API_KEY` and paste the value when prompted. Cloudflare stores it encrypted and never writes it to your config file.


Values under` vars` in the config are plain text, so anything committed there is readable by everyone with repository access. **Put tokens in secrets and keep only non-sensitive settings, such as a base URL, in` vars` .**


### KV, D1 and R2: which binding for which job


Look at KV writes first, because that is the free tier's tightest number:[Free Tier Tracker](https://freetiertracker.com/cloudflare/) lists 1,000 a day. A Worker that updates a counter on every request will hit that in minutes, and later writes fail until the daily reset.


KV reads are 100,000 a day, so it suits configuration that's read often and changed rarely.


Move to D1 and the allowance gets more generous: 5,000,000 rows read and 100,000 rows written per day.


A query that scans a whole table counts every row it touches, so an unindexed lookup can burn through the read allowance faster than the request count suggests.


If you reach for Durable Objects, the allowance is 100,000 operations a day, and for Queues it is 10,000, which caps a queue-based pipeline at 10,000 messages' worth of operations.


> A query that scans a whole table counts every row it touches, so an unindexed lookup can burn through the read allowance faster than the request count suggests.


Purpose Consistency model Free allowance


KV Config, cached lookups, small values read often Eventually consistent; a write can take up to a minute to appear in other locations 100,000 reads/day, 1,000 writes/day, 1 GB


D1 Relational data you query with SQL SQLite database; writes go to a single primary 5,000,000 rows read/day, 100,000 rows written/day, 5 GB


R2 Files and large objects Strongly consistent, S3-compatible 10 GB storage, 1 million writes and 10 million reads per month


Anything you need to read back immediately after writing belongs in D1 or R2, not KV. Anything bigger than a row or a small value belongs in R2.


When a webhook's follow-up work starts eating CPU time and subrequests, the Worker can forward it to an[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) workflow, and the person who needs it doesn't have to be a builder: they describe the process in Activepieces' built-in chat, and what comes out is a published flow in their account, the same kind of flow someone would otherwise assemble step by step.


It sits alongside every other flow there, with the same RBAC, audit logs and run traces, so any run can be opened and read afterwards. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.
